title: Mobilize Finance, Shape Local Markets and Deliver Investment Portfolios
description: This section will include guidance and tools for national, subnational and city governments to mobilize and deploy catalytic funding to test and scale solutions, de-risking mechanisms to support urban climate projects and shape local markets using aggregated procurement.
systemsLogic: Implementing portfolios and pipelines often requires interconnected financing, implementation and market-shaping mechanisms operating together as part of a system. Catalytic and de-risking finance mechanisms can help mobilize investment, while systemic portfolio implementation environments and local climate investment structures and collaborative implementation environments can support coordinated delivery of investments. Procurement complements financing by creating credible demand conditions that allow new solutions to move from demonstrations and small-scale deployment toward wider commercial adoption.

pathways.title: Locally Anchored Multilevel Climate Finance Structures
pathways.whatItIs: Multilevel climate finance structures can be understood as a range of financing arrangements that help municipalities mobilize and deploy capital for climate and transition investment, in collaboration with other levels of government and the private sector. This could include pooled municipal borrowing facilities, trust funds, special purpose vehicles for projects requiring off-balance sheet financing, blended finance arrangements etc. Their purpose is to create a local mechanism for cities to mobilize and deploy climate finance from diverse sources, including national governments, donors or private financiers.
pathways.whyItIsNeeded: In many contexts, the challenge in implementing local climate investments is often not a shortage of capital but matching it to the right portfolio. These finance vehicles and mechanisms can help bridge this gap by connecting portfolios with available capital and can take different forms depending on local government capacity, governance and market conditions.

Lund’s green bond programme is a strong example of a local climate finance structure because it shows how a city can translate climate priorities into a municipally anchored investment vehicle. transferability: considerations

Tailor the financing structure to the local fiscal system, borrowing regulations, tax base and market maturity: where decentralization and private-sector depth are stronger, local trust funds or similar vehicles may work well; where responsibilities are devolved but fiscal space is limited, devolved funds may be a better fit; and in more unitary systems, country- or donor-led funds, like the Viability Fund or LoCAL program, may need to be channelled through existing fiscal transfer mechanisms. In context where local governments have creditworthiness, a green bond framework like Lund could be utilized.

When setting up a climate investment fund, start with a focused investment portfolio, aligned with national priorities and plans, so that investor confidence improves and external finance could be mobilized.

Carefully structure SPVs for project financing and implementation. SPVs are legally complex and expensive downscaling to smaller projects requires careful packaging and de-risking for banks and commercial investors to participate.

Regardless of where the fund gets anchored, enable local planning control while bringing in external capital through multilevel partnerships, so finance supports locally defined and locally led climate priorities.
enablingConditions: Credible leadership, commitment and capacities at various levels of government to structure and manage the climate investment vehicles, or access to an intermediary manager, such as Bristol’s Net Zero Investment Co-Innovation Lab or Tamil Nadu’s subnational government, to support local governments in setting up and managing such funds.
Local alignment with national plans, national platforms and coordination with national institutions for long-term sustainability and ownership

Multilevel partnerships with donors, corporates, individuals, DFIs or national governments to mobilize finance or credible intermediary to hold this mandate, manage these partnerships and channel finance to local investment vehicles.

pathways.title: Innovative and De-risking Financial Tools and Mechanisms
pathways.whatItIs: De-risking financial tools and mechanisms reduce implementation and investment risk while helping mobilize larger pools of public and private capital. This could include concessional finance, guarantees, insurance and blended-finance mechanisms to crowd in investment, strengthen investor confidence and accelerate delivery of priority climate investments. They work best when linked to strong governance, project portfolios and local investment structures.
pathways.whyItIsNeeded: Utilizing innovative and de-risking tools and mechanisms is crucial to mitigate perceived high risks and uncertainties for the investors. Many climate investments at the subnational or local level may be held back not by a lack of ambition, institutional arrangements or political momentum behind them, but by the fact that their risks are too high or too uncertain for private investors to engage at scale. Implementation guidance Working with de-risking and innovative financial mechanisms and tools entails the following activities that multilevel actors can utilize: Identify the main financial risks in the climate investment portfolio. These may include climate impact uncertainties, political risks, low market readiness, currency risks, weak enabling environments, revenue risks, high upfront costs of projects, small ticket sizes etc. Layer appropriate de-risking tool with the specific portfolio risks. For example, credit guarantees could help address revenue or political risks, insurance could de-risk climate impact uncertainties, catalytic capital could help to mitigate early-stage implementation risks, local currency financing could mitigate foreign exchange risk,and aggregation could help avoid low ticket sizes and high upfront costs. Blend public finance, including concessional public or donor finance or guarantees, with private investment such as loans or equities, to crowd-in private investors. Integrate these de-risking tools and blended finance approaches within local climate investment structures, with public institutions helping coordinate and de-risk while private capital enters once risk is acceptable. While structuring de-risking approaches, have continuous coordination between commercial investors, development institutions and governments to leverage each partner’s comparative advantage and maximize impact. What is Blended Finance? Blended finance is the strategic use of a limited amount of concessional public or philanthropic capital to mobilize additional finance, primarily from commercial and private sources — toward sustainable development and climate goals. Rather than a single financial instrument, it is a structuring approach: public actors (donors, development agencies, philanthropies, and development finance institutions) absorb or share risks that would otherwise deter private investors, improving a project's risk-return profile enough to attract market-rate capital. The concessional capital at the core of a blended structure can take several forms, including grants, concessional debt or equity, guarantees, and other risk-sharing facilities. These de-risking mechanisms matter most in emerging markets and developing economies, where country-specific risk accounts for between 60 and 90 percent of investors' risk considerations, and where about 80–90 percent of climate mitigation investment is expected to come from the private sector. The overarching goal is to crowd in private money that would not have been invested otherwise, deploying only as much public subsidy as is needed to make a project viable. Illustrative examples Viability Fund for Cities is a donor-led, catalytic, multilevel funding platform designed to help cities, especially in EMDEs, to move from isolated projects to scalable, investment-ready climate portfolios by linking local investment vehicles with national, regional and international funders. It is built around local investment funds as a key vehicle for channelling co-finance into city-level priorities. The Fund provides limited catalytic capital to support a small number of “game-changing” interventions and creates a shared framework that can be adapted across contexts, including in the EMDEs. Viability Fund’s theory of change is built around three components – align funders across public and private sectors, co-finance priority investments that no single actor would back alone, and aggregate demand through procurement so that demonstrated solutions can move into wider deployment. The Fund aims to partner with key global funders and implementation actors to deploy EUR 10 million by 2030 in co-financing and another EUR 10 million in aggregated demand through a focus on climate-aligned procurement. Viability Fund’s support offer The Viability Fund offers cities two core forms of support. First, catalytic co-financing: through its Co-finance pillar, the Fund will contribute roughly 10 percent of the capital needed for a local investment, taking an early, credibility-anchoring position that is then topped up through national and international co-financing dialogues rather than covering the full cost itself. Second, a local investment fund as a service: because a city must establish its own local climate investment fund, built on shared principles, to receive the Fund's co-financing, the Fund helps set up and run that vehicle, potentially through a fund-manager partner, so it can channel capital to local stakeholders such as solar, batteries, energy infrastructure and SMEs, and recycle returns into harder-to-finance areas like wetlands. Alongside both sits governance and coordination support: aligning funders around common grant principles without pooling capital, and helping cities connect governance, investment planning and procurement — reflecting the Fund's guiding logic that finance follows governance. To know more about with the Viability Fund for cities, click here. Urban Infrastructure Insurance Facility (UIIF) is a multilevel insurance-based risk pooling mechanism involving municipal governments, international donor agencies and city networks. It demonstrates how cities can address climate and disaster exposure risks and protect critical infrastructure. In the UIIF model, ten cities in Latin America and the Caribbean undergo risk assessments that inform tailored insurance coverage and disaster risk reduction measures, with individual city risks transferred into a pooled structure that reduces premiums through economies of scale and risk sharing. After a disaster, cities can access financing more quickly to rebuild infrastructure and support vulnerable residents, while also benefiting from better risk management, legal and technical support, and stronger relationships with financial institutions. UIIF follows a 7-stage roadmap, which includes profiling and selecting cities, assessing risk and tailoring products, designing premium subsidies, tendering the insurance solution, and disbursing the subsidy over time. To know more about UIIF, click here. InfraCredit Nigeria is a strong example of how a local credit-enhancement facility can unlock domestic capital for infrastructure. Established in 2017 through a partnership between PIDG, GuarantCo and the Nigeria Sovereign Investment Authority, InfraCredit provides NGN-denominated guarantees that improve the credit quality of local-currency debt instruments and help projects access longer-tenor finance from institutional investors such as pension funds, insurers and banks that would otherwise not invest. By end-2024, it had guaranteed 24 transactions mobilising over NGN 200 billion in private investment, supported nearly NGN 150 billion in bond issuances, and helped first-time issuers such as North South Power access the domestic capital market. InfraCredit’s portfolio spans projects in Abuja, Lagos, Ondo, Imo, Abia, Cross River, Enugu, Bayelsa, Ado Ekiti and Victoria Island, including solar mini-grids, embedded power, housing, telecoms, a ring road and industrial infrastructure, showing how a national credit-enhancement vehicle can channel finance into a wide range of place-based investments. The model has also been replicated beyond Nigeria through sister facilities in Pakistan, Kenya and Cambodia, with additional markets including Vietnam, Ghana and Francophone West Africa under development or review. To know more about InfraCredit Nigeria, click here. Kommuninvest is a locally led Swedish municipal aggregation mechanism that pools borrowing demand from municipalities and regions, giving them access to capital on more favourable terms. It raises money in the market and on-lends it to its members, operating as a lending-only institution rather than a grant fund or equity vehicle. The model is backed by a joint guarantee from its 282 municipal and 15 regional members, which helps de-risk lending and lower borrowing costs. In 2025, Kommuninvest’s total lending reached SEK 563.9 billion, showing the scale that pooled municipal finance can achieve. To know more about Kommuninvest, click here.

transferability: considerations

Match the financial mechanisms and tools to legal and regulatory conditions, capacities of multilevel actors, risk-return profiles of projects and market maturity. Catalytic funding could be most effective in low-capacity contexts that require initial upfront capital to demonstrate implementation capabilities to crowd in additional finance. Insurance and risk pooling are most transferable where climate-disaster exposure is the main challenge to fiscal resilience; local-currency guarantees fit contexts with a bankable portfolio, where the main constraint is credit quality and investor confidence; pooled borrowing works where municipalities already have a shared financing base and want lower-cost market access or have small ticket sizes and limited creditworthiness to access the market individually.

Replication works best when a trusted intermediary can hold the mandate, coordinate actors and manage risk. For example, Viable Cities plays that coordinating role for the Viability fund, linking it with EU grants opportunities, local trust funds, systems demonstrators etc and the wider multilateral initiatives. Similarly, ICLEI and PIDG play the coordinating, implementation or capacity building roles for UIIF and InfraCredit.

Adopt a phased approach for transferability in lower-capacity contexts. UIIFs’ seven-stage roadmap shows that de-risking instruments are more transferable when they are introduced step-by-step, giving cities and parters time to align data, governance and build capacities progressively. Similarly, Viability Fund also plans to adopt a phased approach, focusing on a few high potential projects, cities and partnerships to demonstrate early success and help inspire other actors to replicate the model.

Embed the tools within existing domestic governance systems, portfolios, investors and financial structures. InfraCredit works well when anchored in a sovereign institution and domestic capital markets to mobilize local institutional investors which would benefit from local currency guarantees. Kommuninvest works well because it is owned jointly by municipalities and is tied to their joint guarantees. Viability fund similarly looks to invest in local investment structures from the outset to maximize the impact of its mobilized funds.
Enabling Conditions

A clear risk profile and a portfolio of investable projects. These tools work best when cities can identify whether the main constraint is credit risk, disaster exposure, foreign exchange risk or early-stage delivery risk, and when there is already a project portfolio that can absorb guarantees, insurance or blended finance.

A legal and regulatory setup that allows the instrument to be deployed. The tools have to align with the regulations for borrowing, guarantees, subsidies, or pooled finance, and public actors need enough budget authority to commit long-term resources to investment portfolios.

Financial structures to absorb capital and integrate innovative financial mechanisms. In contexts where local balance sheets are not strong enough, investment vehicles, like SPVs could be used to integrate mechanisms like aggregation and blended finance.

Risk-bearing capital and counterparties willing to participate. De-risking tools will need first-loss or catalytic capital, a financing partner, and investors prepared to take exposure once risk is reduced. That is visible in KfW/BMZ backing UIIF premiums, and PIDG and NSIA backing InfraCredit to crowd in institutional investors.

pathways.title: Collaborative Portfolio Implementation Environments
pathways.whatItIs: A collaborative portfolio implementation environment is a place-based setup where public, private and civic actors jointly implement, test and adapt a portfolio of mutually reinforcing interventions around a shared transition mission. These place-based initiatives go beyond individual pilots or project-level coordination activities. Instead, they create a shared, ongoing environment where governance, finance, procurement, regulations, organizational cultures and technologies are aligned around a common mission, such as climate action. These implementation environments help generate the evidence, partnerships and institutional changes needed to move successful interventions toward investment and scale.
pathways.whyItIsNeeded: Developing a portfolio and the governance and finance arrangements around it is not sufficient on its own; climate portfolios also need collaborative implementation environments where public, private and civic actors can jointly contribute, deliver, learn and adapt. Without that environment, portfolios can fragment into isolated projects, learning is harder to share, and the system conditions needed for scale do not change.

transferability: considerations

Transfer the core functions of implementation environments, while keeping the institutional form adaptable. The transferable core is a defined local system or place, a shared mission, system mapping, a portfolio approach, continuous orchestration, learning and pathways to finance and scale. The institution leading these functions should reflect the governance context.

Keep implementation locally grounded. Deep transition challenges cannot be solved by externally assembled consortia alone. Local actors with knowledge, mandate, relationships and implementation capacity should anchor the process, while external partners add specialist capabilities. The examples cited above defined their own local priorities, i.e., decarbonization in Lund, land aggregation in Bristol or project preparation for low-carbon building retrofits in Central Asia.

Embed implementation in the institution best placed to provide political mandate, coordination and continuity. Where local governments have sufficient autonomy and capacity (e.g., system demonstrators in Lund, Bristol and Bogota), they can anchor the process directly; where they do not, national ministries, international agencies or other intermediaries (i.e., CCFLA for Local Hubs or a national agency, NIUA, in CITIIS 2.0) can provide the convening power and long-term ownership needed to sustain implementation and scale.

Funding and participation arrangements should fit the governance and institutional context. Whether participating members in a portfolio implementation environment have funded roles, in-kind contributions or voluntary commitments will vary by fiscal capacities, partnership needs and the enabling environments – what matters is that the model is strong enough to sustain engagement and keep the implementation environment moving. For example, the Swedish system demonstrators funded all consortium partners while the local hubs engaged stakeholders without direct funding.

Phase the implementation based on system readiness. In contexts with low readiness levels, implementation should focus on diagnostics, convening, mapping and coalition building (e.g., Central Asia Hub). As readiness increases, focus should shift towards investment planning, testbed selection and portfolio development (see Action 4 for guidance on these). Full implementation should be financed once the mission is co-owned, the coordination function is in place, stakeholders are mobilized, barriers are known and a portfolio is in place.

Use clear, accessible language and simplify the methodology where necessary. The Swedish experience showed that even relatively mature cities struggled when system-demonstrator concepts became overly abstract or innovation-heavy. In lower-capacity contexts especially, guidance should focus on practical functions and outputs rather than specialist transition terminology.

Connect local implementation to national systems from the beginning. Demonstrators are more likely to scale when local evidence can inform national policy, funding programmes, investment priorities and future climate plans. Some System Demonstrators, e.g., in Uganda, have demonstrated that weak national-local institutional connections can constrain scaling even when local demonstration is successful.

Build in a pathway from implementation to scale from the outset. The model is more transferable when it linked from the outset to investment, procurement and replication routes. These pathways may involve national governments, DFIs, PPFs or international donors, depending on the funding context and portfolio readiness. For example, EnergyNet is expected to scale through the Viability Fund, Bristol scaled via the UK Small Sites Aggregator, and Central Asia Hub is expected to scale through project preparation pathways involving Gap Fund, FELICITY II, and financing pathways involving GCF and EIB.
enablingConditions: A political mandate and co-owned decision making between public and private actors.
A dedicated coordination function or intermediary capable of holding the implementation environment together, capture learnings iteratively and
Reliable local data, evidence and a testbed (e.g., a city) so that baseline data and observed barriers could inform implementation.
Flexible and sustained funding for implementation and learning, including resources for orchestration and experimentation, not only capital expenditure on individual assets.

A multilevel pathway for policy and institutional learning, allowing barriers identified in the testbed to be escalated to the regional or national levels and successful approaches to feed into future plans, policies and investment frameworks.
Credible pathways to connect bankable portfolios to finance providers and market-shaping actors, including governments, private developers, investors DFIs and procurement actors.

pathways.title: Aggregated Procurement as a Market-Shaping and Industrial Transition Mechanism
pathways.whatItIs: Aggregated and pooled procurement are a market-shaping and industrial transition mechanisms in which cities, alongside subnational and national agencies and other public and private buyers coordinate purchasing power to create a stronger, aggregated demand for low-carbon and resilience-enhancing goods, services and infrastructure. The market signal can be strengthened further if local procurement activities are aligned with national climate priorities. In this pathway, aggregation can mean multiple buyers coordinating demand while keeping separate budgets and contracts, while pooled procurement combines demand into a single fund or joint tender. The mechanism can operate within a city, across municipalities, or vertically across city, state and national levels.
pathways.whyItIsNeeded: Subnational governments collectively spend over USD 6 trillion a year on goods and services – roughly 8% of global GDP – yet this leverage is fragmented across departments and not coordinated with private demand, so markets receive no stable signal to invest in low-carbon materials. Procurement, when used strategically to align with climate outcomes, can help create a unified, more stable demand for green and resilient infrastructure.

illustrativeExamples.title: First Mover Cities Cohort
illustrativeExamples.excerpt: First Mover Cities Cohort is being developed as a dialogue series by the First Movers Coalition, World Economic Forum. T...
illustrativeExamples.fullText: First Mover Cities Cohort is being developed as a dialogue series by the First Movers Coalition, World Economic Forum. The cohort will bring together city representatives, private actors, and other partners to discuss green procurement governance, tender design, and how to turn fragmented demand into clearer market signals. The cohort is engaging cities such as Stockholm, Seattle and San Francisco, drawing on examples like Stockholm’s tender-based incentives and Zurich’s material-based mandate to show how procurement rules can shift markets for lower-carbon materials, bring public and private actors to coordinate as part of a multistakeholder process. Click here to know more about First Mover Coalition.

illustrativeExamples.title: C40 Clean Construction Accelerator
illustrativeExamples.excerpt: C40 Clean Construction Accelerator shows how city action can move beyond municipal projects and help reshape the wider c...
illustrativeExamples.fullText: C40 Clean Construction Accelerator shows how city action can move beyond municipal projects and help reshape the wider construction market. It is an initiative that brings together eight cities to help transform the building and construction industry. In the accelerator, mayors commit to reusing and retrofitting existing buildings first, leading by example through municipal procurement, demanding transparency through whole-life carbon assessments, building joint roadmaps with stakeholders, approving at least one net-zero flagship project, assessing resilience impacts, and advocating for action at national and higher levels. These commitments translating into practice – cities are using procurement to push whole-life cycle assessments and low-carbon materials, coordinating across departments, working with private-sector partners such as the North American Electric Construction Coalition, and pressing national governments to remove policy barriers.

illustrativeExamples.title: RAMCC Trust Fund, Argentina
illustrativeExamples.excerpt: RAMCC Trust Fund, Argentina demonstrates how a horizontally coordinated pooled procurement vehicles, coordinated horizon...
illustrativeExamples.fullText: RAMCC Trust Fund, Argentina demonstrates how a horizontally coordinated pooled procurement vehicles, coordinated horizontally (i.e., between local governments), can consolidate a fragmented municipal demand into a strong market signal. RAMCC is a coalition of 270 municipalities, and the Trust Fund, established by RAMCC in 2018, helps participating municipalities to finance and deliver projects in their climate action plan by procuring suited climate-smart technologies at lower costs. Each participating municipality is a Trustee and is represented by its mayor in the Assembly of Mayors – a forum for Trustees to set out their project implementation priorities and share progress. The Assembly also elects the executive committee, the Mayor City Council, comprising a group of 5 mayors (one president and four vice presidents), which provides strategic oversight for the Trust’s financing activities each year. A third body, the Executive Secretariat, provides Trustees with technical support to develop climate plans, undertake technical studies, and develop financing proposals. Municipalities approve budgets, pool and allocate funds. The Mayor City Council issues pooled tenders, award contracts and pays technology suppliers. The Trust Fund has initially focused on LED lighting procurement, achieving economies of scale and financial savings and delivering measurable emissions, energy savings.

illustrativeExamples.title: The Grand Challenge, India
illustrativeExamples.excerpt: The Grand Challenge, India is an example of a vertically coordinated (i.e., between multiple levels of government) poole...
illustrativeExamples.fullText: The Grand Challenge, India is an example of a vertically coordinated (i.e., between multiple levels of government) pooled procurement model for urban green transport – a capital-intensive sector. The model aimed to scale up the deployment of e-buses in India and support the transition to low-emissions fleets. Led by Convergence Energy Service Limited (CESL) under the Ministry of Power, and supported by TUMI E-bus Mission, the model pooled demand from multiple cities for e-buses, reduced transaction costs through a single tendering process and used subsidies from the national government, with some state contributions as well. CESL first invited cities to estimate demand and share route, depot and charging information, then consolidated those inputs into a standardized pooled tender. Before issuing the procurement, CESL also consulted OEMs through informal discussions and an initial expression of interest, which helped it test market appetite and adjust the tender design. The tender was then split into five lots with different technical specifications, and bids were selected based on the lowest cost per kilometre. The model relied on a gross cost contract and a mobility-as-a-service structure where private operators own and run the e-buses and charging infrastructure for 12 years, after which they transfer the assets to cities. This helped shift the upfront costs away from cities and suppliers while helping scale a new market for electric buses.

illustrativeExamples.title: Intra
illustrativeExamples.excerpt: Intra-city aggregated procurement in Zurich demonstrates how a city government can leverage its regulatory mandates and ...
illustrativeExamples.fullText: Intra-city aggregated procurement in Zurich demonstrates how a city government can leverage its regulatory mandates and purchasing power to aggregate demand from public and private sectors within its jurisdiction and create a market for low-carbon infrastructure. In 2002, the city began with a pilot showing that a new school could use 80 percent recycled aggregates in concrete, then introduced a 25 percent minimum requirement for recycled aggregates in concrete for new public buildings in 2005 and later tightened its procurement in 2013 to require low-carbon cement as well. Over time, this public procurement approach, together with revisions to Swiss standards and active engagement with local producers, helped create a local market for recycled concrete that later spread into the private sector. As a result, 90% of public concrete used in the city is now recycled (up to 50% recycled aggregates), and between 2016-21, the city’s concrete-related CO₂ emissions were reduced by 25–30% (7,430 tonnes CO₂ emissions saved). Zurich’s procurement policy succeeded in creating a market for recycled concrete that was later spread to the private market, helping aggregate the city-wide demand towards low-emissions infrastructure.

transferability: considerations

Use the procurement model that fits the capacity and governance context. This may be a trust fund with built-in governance, a nationally coordinated tender, or a city-level mandate; the transferable core is the combination of political mandate, technical support, and clear criteria for aggregating demand.

Choose an appropriate procurement jurisdiction based on capacities and governance arrangements. Where cities have strong procurement authority and large infrastructure pipelines, intra-city aggregation can shape markets within one jurisdiction. Where capacities or enabling conditions are weaker at the municipal level, pooling between cities can work, but it usually needs a national intermediary or coordinator to standardize and hold the process together, as in RAMCC and India’s Grand Challenge.

Adapt the procurement objectives based on national climate priorities. For example, cities can focus on procurement models for low-carbon construction materials or e-buses where national priorities include renewable energy and decarbonization, so the market signal reinforces the wider policy direction.
enablingConditions: Clear procurement authority to set procurement rules, define award criteria and, where relevant, coordinate across departments or buyers.
Multilevel coordination capabilities, especially with higher levels of government and the private actors to implement the procurement models
Enabling regulations, procurement frameworks and financing or technical support at the national and subnational levels
Technical capacity within subnational or local governments to design, evaluate and monitor climate-aligned tenders
Early and continuous market engagement to assess readiness of suppliers, manufacturers and other industry actors.
Recommendations for actors: national governments, cities and international partners
